🍎 Lesson plan · 🌱 Basics · Lesson 5

Lesson plan: AI in Everyday Life

The hidden AI you use every day — probably without noticing.

By the end of the lesson, students can

  • find the AI hidden in everyday apps and devices;
  • explain how a recommendation system learns from what you watch, like and skip;
  • explain what a filter bubble is, and name ways to stay in control of a feed.

Warm-up

Think about your day so far. Where might AI have helped you without you noticing?

List the answers. Many students think only of chatbots: the lesson shows how much AI hides in ordinary apps.

Reading

Students read the lesson “AI in Everyday Life”. Students look for three places where AI hides in a phone, and for what a filter bubble is.

Activity: Mini-lab “Spot the hidden AI”

  1. Students open the mini-lab in lesson 5: an ordinary day in six moments.
  2. Before tapping a moment, they guess what AI hides in it and write the guess on the worksheet.
  3. Then they tap the moment, read the answer and check their guess.
  4. Pairs add one more moment from their own day, with the AI hidden in it.

For students who finish early

Fast finishers draw their own day as a timeline with at least four moments of hidden AI.

Discussion questions

  • Your feed is designed to keep you watching. When is that good for you, and when isn't it?
  • Have you ever noticed a filter bubble in your own feed? What could break it?
  • Banks use AI to spot fraud, and doctors use it to read scans. What should happen when the AI is wrong?
  • Which hidden AI in your day would you switch off if you could? Why?

Exit ticket

Name one app you use that recommends things, and one thing it might have learned about you.

Quick check. Your feed shows you more and more videos that match what you already like and believe. What is this called?
Right answer: A filter bubble

Easier and harder

Easier. Give students the names of the six kinds of hidden AI (face recognition, arrival-time prediction, predictive text, spam filter, computational photography, recommendation system) to match with the moments.

Harder. Students write a short guide for a younger student: three signs that a feed is choosing for you, and three ways to take back control.
